--- Jerusalem's Lot.txt ---

[1] Yogsoggoth L91
It is part of the Cthulhu Mythos , inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft and Robert Bloch , and features the town of Jerusalem's Lot, created by King as the setting of his non-Mythos vampire novel 'Salem's Lot "Jerusalem's Lot" was first published in the 1978 collection of King's own short stories Night Shift . It has since been reprinted dozens of times in a plethora of different publications, and has been translated into Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Dutch, Finnish and Chinese. Behind the Mythos De Vermis Mysteriis features heavily in the story, and the godlike creature Yogsoggoth is mentioned. The story functions as something of a follow-on or prequel to King's 1975 vampire novel 'Salem's Lot , linking that tale to the Cthulhu Mythos, although it contains no direct references to it. Taking this story into consideration, it is possible that the undisclosed entity that the villain of 'Salem's Lot makes a pact with might have been Gyyagin , or even Yogsoggoth.

This version is one of the most commonly referenced in the Cthulhu Mythos. In the manga series Alicia Y by Juan Gotō, Dee appears as the main antagonist. He used the Necronomicon to become immortal, and would later get into a conflict with Alicia Y Armitage during his quest to reach godhood. Dee created a homunculus named Errol, who served as his henchman until being sacrificed for the awakening of Cthulhu . Dee ordered Cthulhu to destroy everything in London, with Alicia being caught in one of his tentacles. After heading towards Stonehenge , in order to summon Yog-Sothoth , Dee was seemingly destroyed by Inumaru; however, this actually freed Dee from his bodily prison, liberating him from his mortal self that had been bound to this world and allowing him to reach the domain of Yog-Sothoth. Dee attempted to assimilate himself with Yog-Sothoth but quickly found out that Alicia had already taken the role of Yog-Sothoth, when her consciousness shifted during Dee's summoning of Cthulhu. Alicia took Dee to the grave of the London Tower, the place where he had been sleeping for 111 years before being awoken about half a year ago, killing his past counterpart in front of him, as well as tormenting Dee's spirit with never-ending agony while being unable to lose his mind for eternity.

--- Joseph Curwen.txt ---

This ability is used to obtain privileged intelligence from long-defunct wise men. To this end, his agents scoured the graveyards and tombs of the world for the corpses of illustrious persons, which are then smuggled back to Providence, where Curwen temporarily raised them to torture their secrets out of them. In this endeavour he was assisted by two fellow necromancers and Salem exiles: Simon/Jedediah Orne , alias Joseph Nadek, who lived in Prague; and Edward Hutchinson , who masqueraded as Baron Ferenczy in Transylvania. He was able to summon Cthulhu Mythos entities such as the god Yog-Sothoth to assist him in his magic. Prior to his first death, Curwen found a way to create a spell that would transcend time and inspire a descendant to become interested in him and his work and attempt to bring him back should he ever be slain. When later resurrected by Ward, Curwen initially appeared in disguise as a bearded, spectacled "Dr. Allen" to avoid suspicion, due to his close resemblance to Ward.

He also feigned some degree of civic spirit and decency, both to his fellow citizens and to his wife, as part of a clever ruse—a social gambit aimed at producing an heir, as well as improving his public image to avoid forced displacement. Film Adaptations In the 1963 film The Haunted Palace , Joseph Curwen and his descendant Charles Dexter Ward are both played by celebrated horror actor Vincent Price. Whereas their ultimate goals in the novel are more ambiguous, in the film it is revealed that Curwen and his associates are actually working to bring about the return of Yog-Sothoth, Cthulhu , and other ancient gods. --- Kaalut.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L61
B. Lee Kaalut is a fictional character created by J. B. Lee for the short story " Genuine Article " (January, 1998). Background Kaalut is a gigantic insectoid larva-like horror, dwelling in the nebulous realm of K'gil'mnon , along with the Gharoides , its parasitic insectoid servants. It also likely has human worshipers. Behind the Mythos Kaalut, the Gharoides, and K'gil'mnon were all created by J. B. Lee before he ever read H. P. Lovecraft . Upon discovering the Cthulhu Mythos , Lee decided to incorporate his inventions into the pantheon, mentioning Kaalut along with Yog-Sothoth , Nyarlathotep, Azathoth and Shub-Niggurath in "Genuine Article" (January, 1998).

--- Lord Dunsany.txt ---

[2] Yog-Sothoth L149
There is also a somewhat aimless, dream-like quality to Dunsany's works, which of course the Dreamlands in Lovecraft's writings overtly imitates. Dunsany also populated his fantasy worlds with imaginary gods of various types, as in his first published book, The Gods of Pegāna . The concept of an invented pantheon was a key influence on H. P. Lovecraft, who said he "got the idea of the artificial pantheon and myth-background represented by ' Cthulhu Yog-Sothoth Yuggoth ', etc." from Dunsany. Dunsany also invented creatures, like gnoles and gibbelins, that seem like models for the zoogs and ghasts of Lovecraft's Dreamlands.


--- Lost Stars.txt ---

[1] The Gate L63
It was first published in 2003 in the collection Strange Stars & Alien Shadows: The Dark Fiction of Ann K. Schwader , before being republished in the 2011 anthology The Book of Cthulhu Synopsis A woman named Diane invites her friend Sara to participate in a spirituality group led by the mysterious Egyptian priestess Sesh'tet. Sara works in an art gallery and has been busy organising an Egyptian exposition. Although skeptical, her interest is piqued by the claim that Sesh'tet's religion is older than the cult of Isis. At the meeting, the leader recites excerpts from a book called The Gate of All Lost Stars , which mentions deities with names such as Nyarlat Assatur Shuddam-El Karakossa , and Shuppnikkurat . The principal deity that the text focuses on, however, is the goddess Ammutseba . The priestess Sesh'tet's appearance is peculiar, with disproportionately large eyes and a narrow face. She gives Sara a mystic amulet and instructs her to wear it until their next meeting while focusing her thoughts on whatever goal she wants to achieve. Sara wakes up in the middle of the night to discover that the amulet has attached itself to her skin like a leech. She tears it off with difficulty and tosses it away.

Alvarez Language English Publisher Rogue Planet Press Publication Lovecraftiana Vol 5, Issue 4 Publication date Marble from the Void " is a Lovecraftian short story by author Steven J. Alvarez , first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2021. Synopsis An astronaut performing maintenance work on his ship in the orbit of Saturn encounters a derelict craft. Aboard, he disturbs an entity which opens a portal to another realm, allowing its true form to emerge and unleash its voracious appetites on the galaxy. Trivia Despite never being explicitly named, the entity's description as a collection of glowing spheres locked out of our dimension along with the narrator's reference to it being "both the gate and its key" would suggest that it is intended to be the Outer God Yog-Sothoth


--- Marvel Multiverse.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L133
The One Above All : The master of the Multiverse. It is a mysterious omnipotent being who permits virtually anything to happen in its multiverse, from the birth and creation of new realities to the corruption or destruction of old realities. The Living Tribunal : Balance in the Multiverse is maintained by the Living Tribunal, a being whose power is eclipsed only by the One Above All and who answers only to the One Above All. Eternity (Multiverse) : Similar to how Yog-Sothoth in the Mythos contained within it every universe, likewise the Multiversal version of Eternity also contains within it every universe in the Multiverse. The Firmaments : Beings who embodied the previous Multiverses, with the current Eternity being the Eighth Cosmos (Multiverse). Multiversal Status Quo Powers Organizations and races which controlled territory within the Multiverse or took it upon themselves to defend the Multiverse from a multiversal threat. They went to war to protect what was theirs or to protect the Multiverse from those threatening its existence, and basically functioned as geopolitical factions within the Multiverse. The Congress of Realities : A democracy consisting of representatives from millions of realities.

Countless players have dared to thwart the machinations of Nyarlathotep and plumb the mysteries of the Carlyle expedition . To coincide with the 2010 re-release of the classic 1920s set campaign, Chaosium will also publish the Masks of Nyarlathotep Companion , a tome devoted in its entirety to helping a Keeper run all six chapters of Masks of Nyarlathotep . At over 250,000 words in length, the Companion is larger than the campaign itself and has been a three year labour of love for dedicated fans of both Call of Cthulhu and Masks of Nyarlathotep at the website, yog-sothoth. com. The Companion includes a guide to running each of campaign's six chapters; detailed descriptions of the many tomes and innumerable locations to be found in the campaign; more information about our good friend, Jackson Elias; two extra scenarios set before and during the campaign; adds countless details about the campaign, such as how to handle money, travel, and the replacement of investigators in what is regarded as one of the deadliest of campaigns ever written.

In Lovecraft, the Outer Ones reverence Azathoth, Cthulhu, Lord of the Woods, Nyarlathotep, Shub-Niggurath, Tsathoggua [HPL Whisperer], Yog-Sothoth [HPL Gates], and Ghatanothoa [HPL Aeons].


--- Misquamacus.txt ---

[2] The Lurker at the Threshold L63
P. Lovecraft and August Derleth Misquamacus , also known as Quamis , is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth for their novel The Lurker at the Threshold . While most " posthumous collaborations " credited to Lovecraft and Derleth were entirely written by Derleth, Misquamacus--a Native American leader with great supernatural powers--appeared in a fragment written by Lovecraft and incorporated into a larger narrative by Derleth. The character has since gone on to appear in works by other creators, notably a series of horror novels by the writer Graham Masterton The Lurker at the Threshold One of the few fragments Lovecraft wrote that he never worked into a finished story was a simulated excerpt from a fictional Colonial-era book called Of Evill Sorceries Done in New-England of Daemons in No Humane Shape . It introduces Misquamacus, who is variously described as an "antient Wonder-Worker," an "antient Wizard," a "Wampanaug wise Man," and "head man" of "a Band of Wampanaug Savages." (The Wampanoag are a real-world Indigenous nation that lived somewhat to the south of Lovecraft Country , from what is now the town of Weymouth, Massachusetts , through Cape Cod and to the islands of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard.) [1] Yog L51
(In his house at R'lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.) The horror of Cthulhu is that he is an accurate depiction of the human psyche, which has purposes larger than the here-and-now and is seldom awakened. This story is one of the best descriptions of numinous terror available to man. The other two very strong tales which come from this time are two Randolph Carter pieces, "The Silver Key" and a novel, The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. The first deals with Randolph Carter's urge for a transmundane life, which he gains by acting in accordance with an entity beyond any set of space-time known as Yog-Sototh. This tale and The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath both introduce the urge to go to another world as a heroic urge, and like all such urges they produce great becoming in the hero as he can obtain only images of his quest. In the novel, Randolph Carter seeks to discover the secret of earth's gods, and finds he is descended from them and -- even more to his horror -- has transcended them by his questing. This heroic motif mirrors Lovecraft's own quest for the fantastic.

During this period Alhazred wrote his famous couplet, later included in the Necronomicon (Kitab al Azif): That is not dead which can eternal lie, And with strange Æons even death may die. There is a quaint rumor that he dreamed of the nameless city before writing the couplet. It was probably also during this pilgrimage that he formulated the religious ethics he was to embody in his book. An indifferent Moslem, he worshipped beings whom he called Yog-Sothoth and Cthulhu. The relationship between this religion and the tales of demons in the Empty Quarter is not clear, but is worth noting. Alhazred's ethical system revolved around the Pagan belief in the Jinn. According to Alhazred these jinn, or 'Old Ones' as he calls them, once ruled the Earth, but they warred among themselves until they were overthrown by a rival group (equivalent to the Afrit). Conditions on Earth were change so they could not live, but neither could they die.

[6] Yog-Sothoth L111
A good measure of Strange's power is granted by a group of benevolent deities called the Vishanti, which power the righteous magician can call upon at will. This brings to mind the Derleth dichotomy of the Elder Gods, ultra-powerful, and who, imprisoning the Great Old Ones, have protected mankind. It is not that all the other realms are full of lifeforms desiring the destruction of Earth (although there are plenty of these too!) , rather that there is an incompatibility between the dimensions -- in which the act of breaking the barriers could cause devastation to all the worlds involved!

In 1908, a van der Heyl descendant named Alonzo Typer visited the house in search of the Nameless Thing. His diary recorded his impressions of a number of eldritch entities that he sensed in the house, but it is difficult to be sure which of his experiences pertain to the Nameless Thing, and which to other beings. He found two diaries and a key from Claes van der Heyl; the key was for a lock which Claes had brought from Yian-Ho and which was fixed to a door in the cellar under the house. It is unclear why the van der Heyls locked this door; possibly the Nameless Thing is too dangerous to summon except in specific circumstances, perhaps involving the use of protections. From Claes's diaries, Typer learned a chant to "transfigure that Forgotten One who is Guardian of the Ancient Gateway." It seems that "Forgotten One" is another name for the Nameless thing, for Typer also wrote "I have been rehearsing the Chant that will transfigure the Nameless Thing."

P. Lovecraft Nasht and Kaman-Thah are a pair of fictional characters created by H. P. Lovecraft for his fantasy novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath Description Nasht and Kaman-Thah are bearded, pshent-wearing priests who guard a cavern-temple where a pillar of flame burns. This Cavern of Flame is located just after the gates that separate the Waking World from the Dreamlands , following a stair of seventy steps that dreamers may descend when they enter the realm of dream. After Nasht and Kaman-Thah's station, there is a much longer stair of seven hundred steps, which dreamers may descend in order to pass through the Gate of Deeper Slumber, leading to the Enchanted Wood When Randolph Carter spoke to Nasht and Kaman-Thah about his desire to find Kadath , the priests advised against it, warning Carter that the Gods of Earth would be displeased, and reminding him that no human is aware of Kadath's location. Nephren-Ka is alluded to briefly in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward (1927/1941), in which necromancer Edward Hutchinson signs one of his letters, "Nephren-Ka nai Hadoth, Edw. H." This seems to be some sort of invocation; his colleague Simon Orne signed a letter " Yogg-Sothoth Neblod Zin, Simon O." The most extensive treatment of the character in Lovecraft comes in " The Haunter of the Dark Shining Trapezohedron The Pharaoh Nephren-Ka built around it a temple with a windowless crypt, and did that which caused his name to be stricken from all monuments and records. Then it slept in the ruins of that evil fane which the priests and the new Pharaoh destroyed, till the delver’s spade once more brought it forth to curse mankind.


--- New England.txt ---

[1] The Key L63
Their first colonies were established by religious Puritans at Massachusetts' Plymouth, Boston and Salem . Up through the American Revolution and behind, immigration to New England was dominated by departees from the country that gave the region its name, without the admixture of Dutch and German folk found in the Mid-Atlantic region, or the dependence on enslaved African labor of the Southern colonies. Horror Lovecraft would sometimes suggest that New England was particularly conducive to evoking the feeling of horror that his fiction specialized in. In " The Picture in the House ", the story that first mentions the key Lovecraft Country town of Arkham , Lovecraft declares that the true epicure in the terrible, to whom a new thrill of unutterable ghastliness is the chief end and justification of existence, esteems most of all the ancient, lonely farmhouses of backwoods New England; for there the dark elements of strength, solitude, grotesqueness, and ignorance combine to form the perfection of the hideous. Similarly, " The Colour Out of Space " refers to "farms, ancient and rocky, with squat, moss-coated cottages brooding eternally over old New England secrets". In " The Dunwich Horror Henry Armitage muses: "Unseen things not of earth—or at least not of tri-dimensional earth—rushed foetid and horrible through New England’s glens, and brooded obscenely on the mountain-tops."

--- Ns16rev_E_f0d884ba29.txt ---

[3] Yog-Sothothery L51
Sargent appears in "Corpse Candles." Thomas also pays homage directly to W. Pugmire by setting a story, "Through Obscure Glass," in Pugmire's Sesqua Valley. This was a daring story, I think, because no one can really write with Pugmire's sensuous prose or make the visceral Sesqua Valley come alive like he can. The trilogy of stories that opens the books is set in the Punktown universe; "The Bones of the Old Ones" actually takes place in Punktown. HPL names like Ward and Poe names like Pym appear in some stories. Much of Thomas' approach to the mythos (or Yog-Sothothery if you prefer) is very conventional, the Great Old Ones were cast into imprisonment by the Elder Gods. The Elder Sign has unusual potency against them and their servitors. The grimoires are the usual suspects, except for Thomas' own The Book of Awe and The Metal Book. My summary is that I highly recommend this collection. I think, however, that the stories written later, like "What Washes Ashore" are more deftly written than the earlier ones (well, our favorite authors are always honing their craft, aren't they?) .

[2] Yog-Sothoth L235
He merely pointed to a book of prodigious size which lay open on the table.... HPL The Dreams in the Witch-House Nyarlathotep differs from the other deities in the Mythos in a number of ways. Most of the Outer Gods are exiled to the stars, like Yog-Sothoth and Azathoth, and most of the Great Old Ones are sleeping and dreaming like Cthulhu ; Nyarlathotep, however, is active and frequently walks the Earth in the guise of a human being, usually a tall, slim, joyous man. He has "a thousand" other forms and manifestations, many reputed to be quite horrific and sanity-blasting.

He gains access to the school under the guise of Mister Noyes, an English literature teacher in Wilmarth's absence.

--- Nyogtha_(Cthulhu_Universalis)_bd17182ff2 [Nyogtha (Cthulhu Universalis).txt].txt ---

[2] Yog-Sothoth L19
Источник (URL): Название: Nyogtha (Cthulhu Universalis) Автор: Unknown Источник данных: live-сайт Символов: 2974 Сохранено: 2026-08-25T21:57:36+03:00 SHA-256 контента: e0a7c62044baa0449bf584ea3b27d0042da22710d0954e3c34dd7f283c6db2d9 ТЕКСТ Nyogtha [HK Salem (online text)]: A being spoken of in the Necronomicon as the Dweller in Darkness (2), the Thing that should not be. He dwells in "nighted caverns of hidden foulness." He is referred to as a brother of the "Old Ones." From the context it is not clear which "Old Ones" are referred to: the Old Ones of Yog-Sothoth, the crinoid Old Ones of Antarctica, the humanoid Old Ones of K'n-yan, the Great Old Ones of Cthulhu, or some other grouping. Entry Points and Followers The Necronomicon says that Nyogtha "can be summoned to Earth’s surface through certain secret caverns and fissures, and sorcerers have seen him in Syria and below the black tower of Leng; from the Thang Grotto of Tartary he has come ravening to bring terror and destruction among the pavilions of the great Khan." In 17th century Salem, the witch Abigail Prinn boasted that she was a "high priestess of a fearfully potent god which dwelt deep in the hills," evidently Nyogtha.

--- Of Evill Sorceries done in New England, of Daemons in No Humane Shape (Cthulhu Universalis).txt ---

[1] The Lurker at the Threshold L57
The manuscript begins with the title "Of Evill Sorceries done in New England, of Daemons in No Humane Shape." However, the final page of the account gives a different title, " Thaumaturgicall Prodigies in the New-English Canaan , by the Rev. Ward Phillips , Pastor of the Second Church in Arkham , in the Massachusetts-Bay Boston , 1697." This page describes the birth of a monster child to Goodwife Doten in 1683. It appears that this final page is a continuation of "Of Evill Sorceries," which overall forms a subsection of the larger work, Thaumaturgical Prodigies In Derleth Stories When August Derleth adapted this fragment for use in his novel The Lurker at the Threshold AWD Lurker ], he broke the text into two pieces. He labeled the first two pages as Of Evill Sorceries done in New England, of Daemons in No Humane Shape . However, he treated the final page as an extract from a separate work, Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-English Canaan . This is a conceivable interpretation since the title Thaumaturgical Prodigies appears only on the final page of Lovecraft's manuscript.


--- Of_Evill_Sorceries_done_in_New_England,_of_Daemons_in_No_Humane_Shape_(Cthulhu_Universalis)_a3792bf3df.txt ---

[1] The Lurker at the Threshold L25
However, the final page of the account gives a different title, "Thaumaturgicall Prodigies in the New-English Canaan, by the Rev. Ward Phillips, Pastor of the Second Church in Arkham, in the Massachusetts-Bay. Boston, 1697." This page describes the birth of a monster child to Goodwife Doten in 1683. It appears that this final page is a continuation of "Of Evill Sorceries," which overall forms a subsection of the larger work, Thaumaturgical Prodigies. In Derleth Stories When August Derleth adapted this fragment for use in his novel The Lurker at the Threshold [AWD Lurker], he broke the text into two pieces. He labeled the first two pages as Of Evill Sorceries done in New England, of Daemons in No Humane Shape. However, he treated the final page as an extract from a separate work, Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-English Canaan. This is a conceivable interpretation since the title Thaumaturgical Prodigies appears only on the final page of Lovecraft's manuscript. When Derleth used the fragment, he also made significant textual changes to make it better fit the plot of his novel; notably, Moving the setting from New Plymouth to New Dunnich (Dunwich).

--- Outer God.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L219
Entities such as the extradimensional S'ngac and the primal god Nodens are known to oppose them, and Nyarlathotep's minions are terrified of the latter's. After Lovecraft's death, the concept of the Other Gods was largely replaced with August Derleth 's interpretation of the Great Old Ones, among the ranks of which Derleth included Azathoth and Nyarlathotep, as well as the likes of Cthulhu Yog-Sothoth Hastur Shub-Niggurath Ithaqua , and many others. Derleth gave them an inimical pantheon in the form of the Elder Gods --noted as including Nodens in the story " The Gable Window "--who defeated and imprisoned them.

[2] Yog-Sothoth L259
Although the essence of Derleth's lore remains unchanged, the RPG makes a distinction between deities such as Azathoth and Nyarlathotep (Outer Gods), and others like Hastur and Cthulhu (Great Old Ones), with the former being much more powerful. Sourcebooks such as H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands incorporate the original lore from Lovecraft, clarifying that "Other Gods" is another name for the Outer Gods (although it can also be used specifically for those dwelling in the court of Azathoth, as opposed to the whole pantheon, as well as a number of unaffiliated entities), and acknowledging the Other Gods' protective behaviour towards the Gods of Earth, as well as featuring their cosmic larvae from The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath In addition to Azathoth and Nyarlathotep, other beings recognized as Outer Gods by Chaosium notably include Lovecraft's Yog-Sothoth and Shub-Niggurath, and Clark Ashton Smith Ubbo-Sathla Behind the Mythos The Outer Gods bear a striking similarity to the real-world Gnostic concept of the "Demiurge", a malignant creator being acting in an unconscious and corrupted parody of the "Divine Will", sometimes referred to as "Yaldabaoth", a name which would not seem out of place in the Mythos, and may have influenced the name of Yog-Sothoth List of Known Outer Gods Lovecraft's Works Azathoth HPL The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath The Darkness (Magnum Tenebrosum) HPL Selected Letters 4.617) Gloon HPL The Temple EXP : "The City in the Sea", Mansions of Madness , "Inheritance") Hydra HPL The Horror at Red Hook CIRCLE Hydra EXP Malleus Monstrorum K'thun HPL The Horror in the Museum EXP : "The Madness Out of Time," Lin Carter The Nameless Mist (Magnum Innominandum) HPL Selected Letters 2.303, 4.617; --- Outer_God_The_H.P._Lovecraft_Wiki_Fandom_d6cc1957a0.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L291
Entities such as the extradimensional S'ngac and the primal god Nodens are known to oppose them, and Nyarlathotep's minions are terrified of the latter's. After Lovecraft's death, the concept of the Other Gods was largely replaced with August Derleth's interpretation of the Great Old Ones, among the ranks of which Derleth included Azathoth and Nyarlathotep, as well as the likes of Cthulhu, Yog-Sothoth, Hastur, Shub-Niggurath, Ithaqua, and many others. [2] Yog-Sothoth L295

[3] Yog-Sothoth L301
In addition to Azathoth and Nyarlathotep, other beings recognized as Outer Gods by Chaosium notably include Lovecraft's Yog-Sothoth and Shub-Niggurath, and Clark Ashton Smith's Ubbo-Sathla. Behind the Mythos[] The Outer Gods bear a striking similarity to the real-world Gnostic concept of the "Demiurge", a malignant creator being acting in an unconscious and corrupted parody of the "Divine Will", sometimes referred to as "Yaldabaoth", a name which would not seem out of place in the Mythos, and may have influenced the name of Yog-Sothoth.

[5] Yog-Sothoth L427
In the Doctor Who universe, the Mythos entities are depicted similarly to how Derleth portrayed them, in that there are no Outer Gods or equivalent, and entities such as Yog-Sothoth and Nyarlathotep figure among the Great Old Ones. [1] Yog-Sothoth L47
НАЗВАНИЕ: Outposts ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:26:49 СИМВОЛОВ: 987 Outposts Author William Meikle Language English Genre(s) Horror Publisher Golden Goblin Press Publication Further Tales of Cthulhu Invictus Publication date Outposts " is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle Synopsis During the days of the Roman occupation of the British Isles, an old soldier with an occult background investigates the bizarre deaths of several men on the Antonine wall. As he delves deeper into the mystery, he finds a temple to Yog-Sothoth buried beneath the wall and encounters a crazed Pictish shaman using his dark magic to summon the ancient god. Characters Marcus Caelius , a former legionary with a degree of knowledge on the Elder cults. Flavius Butto , the centurion in command of the targeted wall fort. "Outposts" was first published in the anthology Further Tales of Cthulhu Invictus by Golden Goblin Press in 2017. It was also included in the 2019 collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror

[2] Yog-Sothoth L43
The riots in Ireland, for example. Ex-Minister for the Exterior Whateley's approach had been needlessly heavy handed, as well as dangerously close to nepotism. Northern Ireland was at peace, admittedly, but that was because most of those who had been present at the 2,000 strong Orange Street riots were dead. The remainder were missing, hoped dead, or were gibbering in the already overcrowded asylums that drained most of the health budget nowadays. Yog-Sothoth had brought the warring parties together, as requested, but coroners had paled and turned away from the task of separating the fused mass of flesh that was what remained of the victims, and in the end a mass grave had been the only option. And the anti-Shuggoth prejudice. The National Front had been right, Peabody admitted. Would you want your daughter to marry one? Most of them made fairly good livings as Elvis impersonators and Hollywood stuntmen, their ability to adopt almost any shape making them very popular in certain industrial applications, but the slime and the weird smell and the eyes gave people the creeps.

[3] Yog Sothoth L53
Attempts to persuade the dark worshippers to use less irritating instruments had failed. Great Cthulhu had been welcomed once by nervous initiates with accordian and banjo, and the frozen bodies of the players had been found months later, dropped from a great height onto a moor in the wilds of Scotland. Peabody shivered as he recalled that the banjo seemed to have certain strange alterations . . . And when Yog Sothoth himself, the Key and the Gate, the Gibberer in the insane Space Outside Space and the Time That Was Not Time had coalesced in front of "Everything I Do," a Brian Adams cover band from Glasgow, the carnage had defied description. Thousands were reduced to drooling parodies of human beings, a fetid smoke had filled the air and stung the lungs and teared the eyes, and now Glasgow was a dead city in a blasted wasteland where nothing grew, the sun never shone, and hope and faith and light were dead. Yes, it could have been much worse, admitted Peaboy. It could have happened in a city where somebody would have noticed.

Zap'm'ded's hands were up instantly, forming the Eldritch Circle of Mi-Go-You-Stay.

--- PSEUDOFACTUAL_MATERIAL_BY_THOMAS_V._POWERS_d80835af2a.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L39
An argument can be made that certain aspects or occult practice were taken from the Elder religion, such as the ritual calendar specified in the Necronomicon. It has been speculated that the book was so secretly and surreptitiously circulated that even high church officials were forbidden to read it, if indeed they ever saw a copy, and were content to base their persecutions on local folklore and prejudices of the time. Ironically, the church seemed to have missed most of the few actual reoccurrences of this pantheistic religion (such as in Averoigne, France; where devotees of the Old One Yog-Sothoth are said to have made over one hundred human sacrifices during the 16th and 17th centuries), and instead concentrated on relatively harmless herbal healers, dimwitted practitioners of barely remembered fertility rites, and religious dissenters. In any case, it can be shown now that the worship of Cthulhu and the Elder Gods did exist, and it was extremely ancient and widespread. It is thought from study of anthropological evidence and from what few written records are preserved that widespread belief in the Elder pantheon died out over four thousand years ago in the old world, with the exception of a few shunned and isolated cults.

НАЗВАНИЕ: Pan (Cthulhu Universalis) ИСТОЧНИК: Pan "In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Pan is the god of the wild, shepherds and flocks, rustic music and impromptus, and companion of the nymphs . He has the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat, in the same manner as a faun or satyr . With his homeland in rustic Arcadia, he is also recognized as the god of fields, groves, wooded glens, and often affiliated with sex; because of this, Pan is connected to fertility and the season of spring." [ Pan , Wikipedia] Henry Armitage vaguely compared Pan to Yog-Sothoth when he said "Shew them Arthur Machen’s Great God Pan and they’ll think it a common Dunwich scandal!" [ HPL Dunwich online text )]. The analogy is to the storyline of Machen's story "The Great God Pan," in which Pan impregnates a human woman, who gives birth to an abominable child; just as Yog-Sothoth impregnated Lavinia Whateley , who gave birth to Wilbur Whateley and the Dunwich Horror Phillips Keith identified the Great God Pan as a synonym for Satan , the archetype of evil. Gazing at the creature, Keith experienced what the old priests of Pan used to call ecstasy.

--- Professor Peabody's Last Lecture.txt ---

[2] 'Umr at-Tawil L83
At this point, a storm brews in the summer sky outside. The professor grows visibly nervous, but tries to hide it while continuing to make jokes. Finally, he produces a rare copy of the forbidden Necronomicon that he got from Miskatonic University and starts reading it, casually dismissing the book's warning about the "ghastly consequences". The storm rages while the professor continues to read the book aloud, until he is finally transformed into a monstrous creature before the shocked eyes of his students. Behind the Mythos According to Prof. Peabody, the Great Old Ones include Nyarlathotep 'Umr at-Tawil , Hastur, Cthulhu Azathoth Shub-Niggurath , and Yog-Sothoth . He mentions that their cult has been active as recently as 50 years ago in Arkham , Massachusetts. The three students who ask questions during the lecture are named Mr. Bloch, Mr. Derleth, and Mr. Lovecraft, after seminal Mythos contributors Robert Bloch August Derleth and H. P. Lovecraft . Fittingly, Mr. Derleth is the one who points out that Hastur's name should not be spoken, as it was the real Derleth who came up with the deity's epithet "the Unspeakable". Also fittingly, Mr.

--- Providence (comic book).txt ---

[1] The Key L93
It is set in the same continuity as the " The Courtyard " and the 4-issue Neonomicon series, both also written by Moore. The premise of Providence is that Lovecraft 's stories are loosely based on the experiences of Robert Black, a queer Jewish journalist who is exploring New England in hopes of garnering material for a novel based on occult outsiders. This conceit allows Moore to rework Lovecraft's familiar fictions in his own unique style. --- R'lyeh Text.txt ---

[2] The Key L225
It is unknown whether copies remain extant in other scholarly institutions. In James Ambuehl 's short story " The Advent of Uvhash ", a book titled The R'lyeh Text: Fragmentary Transcriptions is referenced, indicating that in Ambuehl's continuations, at least sections of the original writing remain in existence. In the Demonbane series by Nitroplus, the R'lyeh Text takes the form of a human girl and was located in Innsmouth , where she was guarded by Dagon and the Deep Ones . She was eventually retrieved by the Black Lodge, who used her as one of the key components for their ritual to summon Cthulhu. The R'lyeh Text appears in the Fate franchise by Type-Moon, most notably being featured in the Fate/Zero anime. Although the original translation was in Chinese, it was later translated into Italian as Prelati's Spellbook . Gilles de Rais owns this copy and can use it to summon extra-dimensional sea demons, including the Gigantic Horror.

--- Rhan-Tegoth (Cthulhu Universalis).txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L81
Rhan-Tegoth's victims are crushed and flattened, seared as if with acid, and covered with innumerable circular wounds. Rogers regarded it a god, with himself to be the first priest of its latter-day hierarchy. Rogers expected that it would grant him power in exchange for his sacrifices. Rogers was also afraid that Rhan-Tegoth would die if he did not continue to feed it, and believed that if it dies, the Old Ones can never come back. It is not clear which "Old Ones" are referred to here. However, the grouping may include the following beings, who were either mentioned in Roger's rantings or depicted in the Rogers' Museum Azathoth Chaugnar Faugn Cthulhu Gnoph-Keh Medusa night-gaunts Shub-Niggurath Tcho-Tcho people Tsathoggua , and Yog-Sothoth Rogers believed that Rhan-Tegoth could not be affected by human protections such as pistols. However, after Rogers' death, Orabona somehow killed or otherwise neutralized Rhan-Tegoth. Orabona put the creature on display as a supposed waxwork. However, the authorities considered it too shocking and forced Orabona to stop displaying it. According to Winfield Phillips , Rhan-Tegoth is also known as that "hairy thing," Gnoph-Hek AWD Lurker ]. However, Phillips probably misunderstood a reference to the hairy cannibal Gnophkehs , who also lived in the far north and may have been contemporary with Rhan-Tegoth. --- Rhan-Tegoth_(Cthulhu_Universalis)_6de3104329.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L25
Rhan-Tegoth's victims are crushed and flattened, seared as if with acid, and covered with innumerable circular wounds. Rogers regarded it a god, with himself to be the first priest of its latter-day hierarchy. Rogers expected that it would grant him power in exchange for his sacrifices. Rogers was also afraid that Rhan-Tegoth would die if he did not continue to feed it, and believed that if it dies, the Old Ones can never come back. It is not clear which "Old Ones" are referred to here. However, the grouping may include the following beings, who were either mentioned in Roger's rantings or depicted in the Rogers' Museum: Azathoth, Chaugnar Faugn, Cthulhu, Gnoph-Keh, Medusa, night-gaunts, Shub-Niggurath, Tcho-Tcho people, Tsathoggua, and Yog-Sothoth Rogers believed that Rhan-Tegoth could not be affected by human protections such as pistols. However, after Rogers' death, Orabona somehow killed or otherwise neutralized Rhan-Tegoth. Orabona put the creature on display as a supposed waxwork. However, the authorities considered it too shocking and forced Orabona to stop displaying it. According to Winfield Phillips, Rhan-Tegoth is also known as that "hairy thing," Gnoph-Hek [AWD Lurker]. However, Phillips probably misunderstood a reference to the hairy cannibal Gnophkehs, who also lived in the far north and may have been contemporary with Rhan-Tegoth.

[5] The Key L663
Tussmann had said that he had not read far enough when he had first seen the book. Puzzling over this cryptic phrase I came upon the line he had pored over—marked by his thumb nail. It seemed to me to be another of Von Junzt’s many ambiguities, for it merely stated that a temple’s god was the temple’s treasure. Then the dark implication of the hint struck me and cold sweat beaded my forehead. The Key to the Treasure! And the temple’s treasure was the temple’s god! And sleeping Things might awaken on the opening of their prison door! I sprang up, unnerved by the intolerable suggestion, and at that moment something crashed in the stillness and the death-scream of a human being burst upon my ears. In an instant I was out of the room, and as I dashed up the stairs I heard sounds that have made me doubt my sanity ever since.

[6] The Key L693
The door was locked, and as I hesitated I heard from within a hideous high-pitched tittering and then the disgusting squashy sound as if a great, jelly-like bulk was being forced through the window. The sound ceased and I could have sworn I heard a faint swish of gigantic wings. Then silence. Gathering my shattered nerves, I broke down the door. A foul and overpowering stench billowed out like a yellow mist. Gasping in nausea I entered. The room was in ruins, but nothing was missing except that crimson toad-carved jewel Tussmann called the Key, and that was never found. A foul, unspeakable slime smeared the window-sill, and in the center of the room lay Tussmann, his head crushed and flattened; and on the red ruin of skull and face, the plain print of an enormous hoof. --- Russell's Guide to Interdimensional Entities.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L95
The book focuses on body and alien horror through the lense of B. A. Lee's own Cthulhu -inspired work and mythos, Merrow Tales (2012). Specificities Canon modifications Most entries and descriptions are based on B. A. Lee's own work, Merrow Tales (2012). The bestiary's chapters also follow Lee's personal classification of beings and artifacts into five categories: Great Old Ones , Ascendency, Merrow, Star Spawn, and Subdimensional Entities. The book offers new names for several entities such as the Dunwich Horror (called Dumgal Zi Yog-Sothoth, "Prince of Yog-Sothoth"), Shoggoth (called Gugalushargal, "All Devourer"), Flying Polyp (called Bydogalzul, "Great womb of evil"), Mi-Go (called Star Spawn Drones), and so on. While each entry differentiates between entities sourced from H. P. Lovecraft or Lee's work, it points to Lovecraft as the sole source for entries that offer modifications to the canon. Psionic Alphabet Both Lee and Russell use a fictional alphabet named "psionic alphabet" in illustrations and occasionally in the text, mostly as a depiction of "true names". The alphabet is a phonetic collection of characters directly linked to English letters and diphtongs. Each letter, regardless of its use and placement in a word, possesses individual variations resembling small tentacles.

[2] Yog-Sothoth L89
Y. N. Freaks Haiyore! Nyaruko-san Fate/Grand Order The Scimitar of Barzai (also known as Barzai's Scimitar ) is a fictional artefact in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos . It was first mentioned in George Hay's anthology The Necronomicon: The Book of Dead Names , which describes the recipe for the item. It is named after Barzai the Wise from H. P. Lovecraft 's short story " The Other Gods "; however, it is unknown if the Scimitar has any connection to its namesake. Description According to the Necronomicon , the Scimitar of Barzai is a bronze scimitar that has the power to summon the Outer God Yog-Sothoth . In the day and hour of Mars, and when the Moon increases, the Scimitar should be made with a hilt of fine ebony, along with arcane symbols inscribed on each side of the blade. After the ritual is complete, the Scimitar must be wrapped in a cloth of black silk and set aside until it is used again. If anyone else tries to abuse the Scimitar's power, it will be rendered powerless.

[3] Yog-Sothoth L129
After Tiberius summoned his Deus Machina known as Belzebuth, Kurou summoned a gigantic version of the Scimitar while piloting Demonbane. On an island near Innsmouth , Kurou used the Scimitar to fight off a pair of human-octopus hybrid monsters at the stone temple. Despite their regeneration capabilities, Kurou figured out how to defeat the monsters by surrounding them in a whirlwind of pages, using flames from the Scimitar to envelope the monsters in a whirling inferno. Later, during the final battle, the Demonbane trio used the Scimitar to trace Master Therion after they entered Yog-Sothoth's gate EXP Deus Machina Demonbane

НАЗВАНИЕ: Servitor of the Outer Gods ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:28:04 СИМВОЛОВ: 1764 Servitor of the Outer Gods Sociocultural Characteristics Also known as Flute-players Idiot Flute-players Amorphous Flute-players Affiliations Outer Gods Real World Information First appearance HPL The Rats in the Walls Appearances AWD The Lurker at the Threshold Created by H. P. Lovecraft The Servitors of the Outer Gods , also known as the Idiot Flute-players or Amorphous Flute-players , are a fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos . They were first referred to by H. P. Lovecraft in his short story " The Rats in the Walls ", and are also featured in August Derleth 's stories, such as The Lurker at the Threshold The Servitors of the Outer Gods were later incorporated into Chaosium 's roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu EXP Malleus Monstrorum Background The Servitors of the Outer Gods are amorphous beings that resemble squids, frogs, and octopi which are constantly changing their shape and appearance. When needed they accompany the Outer Gods, though most of them are in the Court of Azathoth The music to which the Outer Gods dance to is made by these demonic drummers and flautists. On occasion they will also play for cultists to summon deities or to provide background music.

--- Shadows of Yog-Sothoth.txt ---

[3] Yog-Sothoth L83
Overview The first scenario supplement for Call of Cthulhu Shadows of Yog-Sothoth contains a seven-part campaign and two stand-alone adventures. The campaign takes the players across the globe in pursuit of the cult of the Hermetic Order of the Silver Twilight , from America ’s east coast to Scotland to the South Pacific. The two adventures consist of "The People of the Monolith", a trip to Hungary in search of a mysterious poet, and "The Warren", the hunt for a missing friend in Boston. Released in 1982, the first edition of Shadows of Yog-Sothoth ran to 72 pages and featured artwork by Tom Sullivan . In 1989, it was collected along with other previously-published playing material and an all-new scenario in Cthulhu Classics , while in 2004, it was re-released in an updated format for the sixth edition of Call of Cthulhu along with new material and artwork. This version ran to 144 pages.

Beyond them, the graveyard was choked with a thick mist. My headlights bounced off the cloud, making it look like a solid, whitewashed wall; we couldn't even see the nearest headstones. Unfortunately, there was no one around to greet us and neither Michele nor I wanted to get out and start knocking on doors. Yet we also were not willing to leave immediately. --- Spawn of Yog-Sothoth.txt ---

[2] Yog-Sothoth L77
P. Lovecraft The Spawn of Yog-Sothoth are fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos . First appearing as the Dunwich Horror from H. P. Lovecraft eponymous short story , they were later incorporated into Chaosium 's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu EXP Ye Booke of Monstres Background The Spawn of Yog-Sothoth are thoughtless squirming masses of flesh, tentacles, eyes, and tails, along with extra maws in places where joints or vertebrae would be expected. They are amorphous and can fit through most gaps, pulling themselves through with tentacles. They notably emanate an unpleasant scent, typical among old ones and relations. In addition, they possess a weak form of invisibility, allowing them to pass in the dark without drawing attention.

[3] Yog-Sothoth L83
In addition, they possess a weak form of invisibility, allowing them to pass in the dark without drawing attention. They quickly grow to enormous size, and if they continue to feed, they will continue to grow but at a much slower rate. Despite this, their cognition never improves to be much more developed than that of a toddler. Due to this, they are not capable of complex decision making, more motivated by short term instincts than the Child of Yog-Sothoth , a closely related species. They are capable of wielding magic, but rarely use it for more than fundamental rites. The ancient Spawn of Yog-Sothoth can be as large as buildings or small hills; however, they are generally dormant at this size to preserve energy. If killed, their flesh rapidly melts, and soon only a crusty stain remains.

НАЗВАНИЕ: Spoonhead ИСТОЧНИК: ДАТА: 2026-06-15 03:29:14 СИМВОЛОВ: 1090 Spoonhead Created by The Great Intelligence Used by The Great Intelligence Type Data Storage and Transmission Real World Information Creator Steven Moffat First Appearance ADJ The Bells of Saint John The Spoonheads are fictional robots created by the BBC for the Doctor Who storyline The Bells of Saint John , which first aired in 2013. Background The Spoonheads are robots which were created to assist the Great Intelligence (also known as Yog-Sothoth ). They were roughly humanoid in shape though metallic, with a spoon-shaped head and angular limbs. The back of the head was an upload panel which virtualized people into incorporeal forms. While in its camouflaged mode, it looked human, except for the back of the head. It used a holographic projection to camouflage itself, using the images of the subconscious of the individuals looking at it to create its disguise. Described by the Doctor as a "walking Wi-Fi base station" that "hoovered up people".

--- Stories_0ae089fca6 [Librarium Cthulhuvius_3.txt].txt ---

[1] The Lurker at the Threshold L55
S. T. Joshi has published his reading of the text in H. P. Lovecraft, Collected Fiction Volume 3 (1931-1936): A Variorum Edition. Joshi suggests the fragment is from the mid-1930s. The title Of Evill Sorceries done in New England, of Daemons in No Humane Shape occurs at the beginning of the first page, and the publishing information for Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-English Canaan occurs on the final page. Joshi interprets Of Evill Sorceries as being an extract from the longer work Thaumaturgical Prodigies. When August Derleth adapted this fragment for use in his novel The Lurker at the Threshold, he broke the text into two pieces. He labeled the first section as Of Evill Sorceries done in New England, of Daemons in No Humane Shape. However, he treated the final page as an extract from a separate work, Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-English Canaan. This is a conceivable interpretation since the title Thaumaturgical Prodigies appears only on the final page of the manuscript.

--- Stories_2414430e39 [H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth, The Survivor.txt].txt ---

[3] Yog-Sothoth L1121
Charriere and his belief a strange and provocative corroboration. Yet the surgeon had not often gone beyond the realm of pure conjecture. What he sought seemed to be the connecting link among the various instances which had come to his notice. He had sought this link in three bodies of lore. The most familiar of these was the vodu legendry of Negro culture. Next to it, in familiarity, stood the animal worship of ancient Egypt. Finally, and most important, according to the surgeon’s notes, was a completely alien culture which was as old as earth, nay, older, involving ancient Elder Gods and their terrible, unceasing conflict with equally primeval Old Ones who bore such names as Cthulhu, Hastur, Yog-Sothoth, Shub-Niggurath, and Nyarlathotep, and who were served in turn by such curious beings as the Tcho-Tcho People, the Deep Ones, the Shantaks, the Abominable Snow Men, and others, some of whom appeared to have been a sub-order of human being, but others of which were either definite mutations or not human at all. All this fruit of Dr. Charriere’s research was fascinating, but in no case had he adduced a definite, provable link. There were certain saurian references in the Vodu cult; there were similar connections to the religious culture of ancient Egypt; and there were many obscure and tantalizing suggestions connecting the saurians to the Cthulhu myth-pattern, ranging far deeper into the past than Crocodylus and Gavialis, embracing Tyrannosaurus and Brontosaurus, Megalosaurus, and other Mesozoic reptilia.

The yellowed county records containing her testimony and that of her accusers were so damnably suggestive of things beyond human experience—and the descriptions of the darting little furry object which served as her familiar were so painfully realistic despite their incredible details. That object—no larger than a good-sized rat and quaintly called by the townspeople "Brown Jenkin"—seemed to have been the fruit of a remarkable case of sympathetic herd-delusion, for in 1692 no less than eleven persons had testified to glimpsing it.

The small tombs have their chapels contained in their stone mastabas or superstructures, but the mortuary chapels of the pyramids, where regal Pharaohs lay, were separate temples, each to the east of its corresponding pyramid, and connected by a causeway to a massive gate-chapel or propylon at the edge of the rock plateau. The gate-chapel leading to the Second Pyramid, nearly buried in the drifting sands, yawns subterraneously southeast of the Sphinx. There are unpleasant tales of the Sphinx before Khephren—but whatever its elder features were, the monarch replaced them with his own that men might look at the colossus without fear.

The books were old, but the books were not dusty. They had been read— "Read them?" It was as though Canning divined my inmost thoughts. He had put aside his flute and now approached me, tittering as though in continued drunken defiance of the storm. Odd echoes and boomings now sounded through the long halls of the house, and curious grating sounds threatened to drown out his words and his laughter. "Read them?" said Canning. "I study them. Yes, I have gone beyond grandfather and father, too. It was I who procured the books that held the key, and it was I who found the key. A key more difficult to discover, and more important, than the key to the vaults below. I often wonder if Poe himself had access to these selfsame tomes, knew the selfsame secrets. The secrets of the grave and what lies beyond, and what can be summoned forth if one but holds the key." He stumbled away and returned with wine. "Drink," be said. "Drink to the night and the storm." I brushed the proffered glass aside. "Enough," I said. "I must be on my way."

But I promise to keep you informed over the telephone of every move—you see I’ve enough wire here to reach to the centre of the earth and back!" I can still hear, in memory, those coolly spoken words; and I can still remember my remonstrances. I seemed desperately anxious to accompany my friend into those sepulchral depths, yet he proved inflexibly obdurate. Then he shook my hand, shouldered the coil of wire, and disappeared within that indescribable ossuary.

--- Stories_9065b7e62e [H. P. Lovecraft, Ex Oblivione.txt].txt ---

[2] The Gate L45
When I saw this lore, I knew that it touched on the scenes I had haunted, and I therefore read long in the yellowed papyrus. Some of the dream-sages wrote gorgeously of the wonders beyond the irrepassable gate, but others told of horror and disappointment. I knew not which to believe, yet longed more and more to cross forever into the unknown land; for doubt and secrecy are the lure of lures, and no new horror can be more terrible than the daily torture of the commonplace. So when I learned of the drug which would unlock the gate and drive me through, I resolved to take it when next I awaked. Last night I swallowed the drug and floated dreamily into the golden valley and the shadowy groves; and when I came this time to the antique wall, I saw that the small gate of bronze was ajar. From beyond came a glow that weirdly lit the giant twisted trees and the tops of the buried temples, and I drifted on songfully, expectant of the glories of the land from whence I should never return.

[3] The Gate L49
Last night I swallowed the drug and floated dreamily into the golden valley and the shadowy groves; and when I came this time to the antique wall, I saw that the small gate of bronze was ajar. From beyond came a glow that weirdly lit the giant twisted trees and the tops of the buried temples, and I drifted on songfully, expectant of the glories of the land from whence I should never return. But as the gate swung wider and the sorcery of drug and dream pushed me through, I knew that all sights and glories were at an end; for in that new realm was neither land nor sea, but only the white void of unpeopled and illimitable space. So, happier than I had ever dared hoped to be, I dissolved again into that native infinity of crystal oblivion from which the daemon Life had called me for one brief and desolate hour. [4] Yog-Sothoth L587
For many nights Phillips did not light the lamp. The nights lengthened into months, the months into years. He grew older, and his fictions found their way into print, and the myths of Cthulhu; of Hastur the Unspeakable! of Yog-Sothoth; and Shub-Niggurath, the Black Goat of the Woods with a Thousand Young; of Hypnos, the god of sleep; of the Great Old Ones and their messenger, who was Nyarlathotep—all became part of the lore of Phillips’ innermost being, and of the shadow-world beyond. He brought Arkham into reality, and delineated the strange high house in the mist; he wrote of the shadow over Innsmouth and the whisperer in darkness and the fungi from Yuggoth and the horror at Dunwich; and in his prose and verse the light from the lamp of Alhazred shone brightly, even though Phillips no longer used the lamp.

[4] Yog-Sothoth L879
As in many cultures, the Elder Gods were not often named; the Ancient Ones were, and often, for they were still worshipped and served by followers throughout earth and among the planetary spaces; and they were aligned not only against the Elder Gods, but also against one another in a ceaseless struggle for ultimate dominion. They were, in brief, representations of elemental forces, and each had his element—Cthulhu of water, Cthugha of fire, Ithaqua of air, Hastur of interplanetary spaces; and others among them belonged to great primal forces—Shub-Niggurath, the Messenger of the Gods, of fertility; Yog-Sothoth, of the time-space continua, Azathoth—in a sense the fountain-head of evil. Was this pattern after all not familiar? The Elder Gods could so easily have become the Christian Trinity; the Ancient Ones could for most believers have been altered into Sathanus and Beelzebub, Mephistopheles and Azarael. Except that they were co-existent, which disturbed me, though I knew that systems of belief constantly overlapped in the history of mankind.

--- Supernatural (TV show).txt ---

[2] The Gate L125
Yokoth Yokoth, featured in Season 13, Episode 17, is a god from a parallel universe, described by one of the special effects artists who worked on the show as a "tentacle monster." She was summoned to Earth in a ritual held in Rhode Island in , and imprisoned in the body of a human woman. Inadvertently released by the Winchesters, she reopens the rift between her dimension and Earth so that her mate Glythur can join her in devouring Earth's universe. Sam and Dean manage to close the rift to stop the manifestation of Glythur, who pulls Yokoth back into their own universe with his tentacles as the gate is sealed. Yokoth describes herself as the "Star of madness. Ravager of galaxies. Mother of faceless hordes." She and Glythur have consumed most of their own universe, leading them to seek entry into Earth's continuum. Yokoth's name evokes both Yog-Sothoth and Yuggoth . Episode writer Davy Perez, however, has said (in a since-deleted tweet) that her name combines " Shoggoth " with the name of another Supernatural writer, Steve Yockey. Glythur, meanwhile, blends " Hastur " with show writer Meredith Glynn.

--- The Black Brat of Dunwich.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L77
Sargent , first published in issue #10 of the zine Cthulhu Codex in 1997. It retells the story of H. P. Lovecraft 's " The Dunwich Horror " from a different perspective, painting Wilbur Whateley in a far more sympathetic light, and conversely Henry Armitage as the story's villain. Synopsis Two men writing the first definitive account of the Dunwich horror of 1928 encounter an old man who claims to have been employed for a time as Wilbur Whateley's tutor. He reveals the truth of those events: that Henry Armitage and Old Whateley were working together to bring about the return of the Outer God Yog-Sothoth , along with Wilbur's loneliness as a pariah and reluctance to be a part of the plot. After his grandfather's death, Wilbur worked tirelessly to find a way to contain of perhaps even destroy his brother. Horror historian Les Daniels called The Case of Charles Dexter Ward Lovecraft's "finest novel". E. F. Bleiler noted that the short novel, "despite its being strangely tired and routine, has interesting concepts and good moments". Douglas Robillard stated Lovecraft's negative assessment of The Case of Charles Dexter Ward was "too harsh; this is one of his finest works". Cthulhu Mythos Charles Dexter Ward contains the first mention of the Cthulhu Mythos entity Yog-Sothoth , who appears repeatedly as an element in an incantation. Joseph Curwen is the owner of a copy of the Necronomicon (disguised as a book labelled Qanoon-e-Islam ) and there are hints of cult activities in a fishing village that refer obliquely to the events narrated in " The Festival ". The story also contains references to the Dream Cycle : Dr. Willett notices the " Sign of Koth " chiselled above a doorway, and remembers his friend Randolph Carter drawing the sign and explaining its powers and meaning. First appearance of the Dragon's Head and Dragon's Tail signs.

There, he discovers a series of diaries which reveal that the Fells were a clan of cultists in service to many dark gods , including Cthulhu Yog-Sothoth , and Dagon . They also tell of how Vanessa's death was no accident, merely the first part in a ritual which will allow her to join with her gods, as long as a sacrifice can be provided.

Plot summary In the isolated, desolate, decrepit village of Dunwich, Wilbur Whateley is the hideous son of Lavinia Whateley , a deformed and unstable albino mother, and an unknown father (alluded to in passing by mad Old Whateley , as " Yog-Sothoth "). Strange events surround his birth and precocious development. Wilbur matures at an abnormal rate, reaching manhood within a decade. Locals shun him and his family, and animals fear and despise him (due to his odor). All the while, his sorcerer grandfather indoctrinates him into certain dark rituals and the study of witchcraft .

[2] Yog-Sothoth L287
Wilbur matures at an abnormal rate, reaching manhood within a decade. Locals shun him and his family, and animals fear and despise him (due to his odor). All the while, his sorcerer grandfather indoctrinates him into certain dark rituals and the study of witchcraft . Various locals grow suspicious after Old Whateley buys more and more cattle, yet the number of his herd never increases, and the cattle in his field become mysteriously afflicted with severe open wounds. Wilbur and his grandfather have sequestered an unseen presence at their farmhouse; this being is connected somehow to Yog-Sothoth. Year by year, this unseen entity grows to monstrous proportions, requiring the two men to make frequent modifications to their residence. People begin to notice a trend of cattle mysteriously disappearing. Wilbur's grandfather dies. His mother disappears soon afterwards. The colossal entity eventually occupies the whole interior of the farmhouse. Wilbur ventures to Miskatonic University in Arkham to procure their copy of the Necronomicon — Miskatonic's library is one of only a handful in the world to stock an original.

She is described as a somewhat deformed, unattractive albino woman... a lone creature given to wandering amidst thunderstorms in the hills and trying to read the great odorous books which her father had inherited through two centuries of Whateleys.... She had never been to school, but was filled with disjointed scraps of ancient lore that Old Whateley had taught her.... Isolated among strange influences, Lavinia was fond of wild and grandiose day-dreams and singular occupations. Elsewhere, she is called "slatternly [and] crinkly-haired". In 1913, she gave birth to Wilbur Whateley by an unknown father, later revealed to be Yog-Sothoth . Presumably, she is either forced or coerced into mating with Yog-Sothoth by her father, Old Whateley. On Halloween night in 1926, she disappeared under mysterious circumstances, most likely killed or sacrificed by her son, whom the villagers claimed had an immense dislike of Lavinia. Realizing his bluff has run its course, the narrator moves to another. This time, he appeals to the stranger's cultist side, and pretends to be the human messenger or incarnation of an Aztec god. The stranger is so overcome by this display that their frantic worshipping pulls the battery off the seat, and it strikes the ground, causing the mask to activate and kill the stranger. This horrible death is so shocking to witness that the narrator faints. Forty years later, the narrator still does not know what truly happened in the train car: a stress dream, astral projection, or some other explanation. He wonders if Feldon was truly in the car, or if he, the narrator, was somehow in the cave in Mexico?

--- The Gods of Pegāna.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L57
B. Yeats, James Joyce, and Ezra Pound, among others. The book is organized as a series of sketches about an imaginary pantheon; the concept was a key influence on H. P. Lovecraft , who said he "got the idea of the artificial pantheon and myth-background represented by ' Cthulhu Yog-Sothoth Yuggoth ', etc." from Dunsany. Dunsany published a sequel, Time and the Gods , in 1906. The Pantheon The creator of the gods is MĀNA-YOOD-SUSHĀЇ , "the god of Having Done and of the Resting." After creating the gods, he went to sleep, and when he awakes again, it will be the end of the gods and all worlds. He is the one god man cannot pray to. Skarl, the Drummer, attends MĀNA-YOOD-SUSHĀЇ, playing his drum to keep him asleep.

--- The Larkhill Barrow.txt ---

[1] The Gate L51
Synopsis Famous occultist Thomas Carnacki is summoned to assist a military man with a problem his unit have been having at their training facility: every time they test a new machine gun atop a rise in the ground, it results in the shooter going insane (an effect which dissipates after a short time) and the whole camp suffering from dreadful dreams of drums - and something far more sinister - in the dark (which does not). Carnacki's investigations revealed that the rise is in fact an ancient barrow designed as a kind of sonic prison for an ancient and malevolent entity, and the rhythmic drum of the machine gun has partially opened the gate. Luckily for everyone, Carnacki is able to reproduce the effects of the prison through the use of phonograph recordings and many mystical charms, and even manages to re-incarcerate the entity on one of his phonograph cylinders, a fact he keeps hidden from everyone involved. Characters Thomas Carnacki , a renowned occult detective. Private Jimmy Carruthers , a brave 18 year old soldier who assists Carnacki in his efforts. The Lurker at the Threshold was a small box expansion pack for Arkham Horror Second Edition Fantasy Flight Games ' board game of Lovecraftian adventure. Overview As a small-box set, The Lurker at the Threshold was a cards-only expansion, featuring 56 Investigator cards including new Items and Spells, and 110 Ancient One cards whose special effects were intended to spin games of Arkham Horror in different directions from the core set. In addition, this pack saw the introduction of the Relationship and Dark Pact mechanics to Arkham Horror. As its name might suggest, the Relationship mechanic allowed players to develop interpersonal relationships with one another, further enhancing the role-play aspect of the game, while the Dark Pact rules allowed players to make beneficial, but potentially highly costly, deals with the Lurker at the Threshold. Behind the Mythos "The Opener of the Way" was not included in the first two editions of Mysteries of the Worm , reflecting its subtle connection to the Cthulhu Mythos. Referring to Sir Ronald's parchment and the Egyptian priest who wrote it, the story states: The enchanter who had written it alluded to gods far older than those he worshipped. There was mention of the 'Demon Messenger' and the 'Black Temple', coupled with the secret myth and legend-cycles of pre-Adamite days. While in the parchment, the "names of these accursed ones were set forth", they are not specified in the story.

[3] The Opener of the Way L95

--- The Silver Key.txt ---

[1] The Key L95
Hoffmann Price The story and its sequel both feature Lovecraft's recurring character of Randolph Carter as the protagonist. Synopsis silver key in his attic, inscribed with mysterious arabesque symbols, which he finds and takes with him on a visit to his boyhood home in the backwoods of northeastern Massachusetts (the setting for many of Lovecraft's stories), where he enters a mysterious cave that he used to play in. The key somehow enables him to return to his childhood as a ten-year-old boy, and his adult self disappears from his normal time. The story then relates how Randolph's relatives had noted, beginning at the age of ten, that he had somehow gained the ability to glimpse events in his future. The narrator of the story then states that he expects to meet Randolph soon, in one of his own dreams, "in a certain dream-city we both used to haunt", reigning there as a new king, where the narrator may look at Randolph's key, whose symbols he hopes will tell him the mysteries of the cosmos.

It was first published in Carter's 1980 collection Lost Worlds Synopsis The story purports to be part of Prof. Copeland 's translation of the Zanthu Tablets , which narrate the life of the hierophant Zanthu , high-priest of the god Ythogtha in the ancient continent of Mu . Peppered through the text are Copeland's footnotes, which provide additional information about many beings and places mentioned by Zanthu. About 11,000 years after the time of T'yog , the cult of the god Ghatanothoa becomes the sole official religion of the kingdom of K'naa , thanks to the influence of its high-priest Yaa-Thobboth over King Shommog. This results in all the other temples being sealed and the worship of other deities being banned. Given the political power of K'naa, Zanthu fears that the same law might be passed in his own kingdom, G'thuu. Zanthu's palace is located next to the Abyss of Yhe , where Ythogtha himself is believed to be imprisoned by the Elder Sign placed there by the Elder Gods . Studying the Thirty-one Rituals , Zanthu finds a spell that could open the door of Yhe and liberate his god from its prison.

[2] The Gate L125
At first, Zanthu is awed by the sight of a faceless, mountain-sized creature with a single black horn that emerges from the pit. But when a second identical "monster" emerges next to it, followed by many others, Zanthu cries in fear as he realises the sheer size of the creature. The things he mistook for individual monsters are nothing more than the tips of Ythogtha's clawed fingers. Zanthu and his acolytes run away while the earthquakes caused by Ythogtha's movements destroy the continent of Mu. The Elder Gods descend to Earth from Betelgeuse as great towers of flame to push the monster back into the abyss and close the gate. Zanthu and a few others manage to reach a "sky chariot" and escape, but watch their homeland sink beneath the waves. In his final rant, Dan alternates between reaffirming his loyalty to Yog-Sothoth and proclaiming his innocence, blaming the woman's death on the whippoorwills.

Меня зовут Александр Флетчер, и для стороннего взгляда я до самого недавнего времени вёл тихое, учёное существование, посвящённое исследованиям и знанию, существование, которое лишь продолжало увлечённость архаичным и древним, занимавшую меня с самых ранних лет, когда во время многих мальчишеских прогулок по сельской местности, окружавшей место моего рождения в Дорсете, я натыкался то на кремнёвый наконечник стрелы, то на загадочный костяной инструмент, оставленный доисторическими обитателями той земли, и обнаруживал, что моё воображение воспламенено мыслями о минувших глубинах истории, сокрытом знании и первобытной легенде. Из столь скромных начал и произросло моё призвание, и когда наконец я поступил в колледж, я направил свои занятия в область археологии. И мои особые интересы, которые к тому времени сосредоточились на дразнящих намёках на земные, но дочеловеческие разумы, различимые в изречениях некоторых древних клинописных табличек древнего Шумера, не остались без некоторого внимания (и известного цоканья языками) со стороны моих профессоров.

[6] Той L71
Я действительно жаждал увидеть его снимки, но сильно беспокоился о том воздействии, которое эти образы могли бы оказать на меня, и удивлялся, что мой студент избежал какого-либо видимого влияния. Однако он не выказывал ни следа тревоги, за исключением мимолётного замечания, что по пути из музея на лондонский вокзал, а затем от кембриджского вокзала до своего жилья он чувствовал, будто за ним следят. Но он весело сообщил мне, что намеревается проявить свои плёнки в своей крошечной тёмной комнате той же ночью и что фотографии будут готовы для моего просмотра на следующий день после полудня, в каковое время он настоятельно просил меня навестить его. Он закончил наш разговор заявленным намерением начать свою химическую работу без промедления, но с глубоким чувством дурного предчувствия я шёл к его жилью на следующий день; увидев полицейского на лестничной площадке перед его комнатами, моё сердце упало. Моя тревога о ментальном благополучии моего студента была, однако, неуместна, ибо, скорее, его физическое существо было безжалостно уничтожено.

[8] Той L113
Таким вот образом я добыл информацию, критически важную для моего первого активного осуществления моей мести, ибо с помощью определённых техник убеждения я вытянул из некоего самозваного верховного жреца личности людей, которые помогали разуму, столь надругавшемуся надо мной, и которые, более чем вероятно, сыграли главную роль в уничтожении моего чрезмерно увлечённого студента. Я вернулся прямо в Англию после той встречи, с душой, непоправимо запятнанной как воспоминаниями о действиях, которые я был вынужден совершать, так и знанием о действиях, которые я намеревался осуществить, но, тем не менее, тёмно пылающий предвкушением.

[9] Той L147
Поистине, ощущение боли и страха, излучавшееся этим кощунственно составным существом, прежде чем оно вырвалось на свободу и проломило себе путь из моей лаборатории, является, по моему мнению, более чем адекватной компенсацией за любое беспокойство или страдание, которые я могу испытать до или во время моей окончательной кончины. То, что моя кончина наступит скоро, я не сомневаюсь. Сама сущность, не целиком состоящая из той субстанции, что формирует основу нашего материального мира, необъятно сильна и мощно вооружена. По большей части она невидима для человеческих глаз и, заряженная мощной ментальной способностью Великой Расы, она хитра и продуманна далеко за пределами человеческих возможностей. То, что она ещё не расправилась со мной — поистине, то, что она не перебила всё население Аркхэма и не опустошила окружающую сельскую местность, — приписываемо лишь врождённому нежеланию Великой Расы отнимать жизнь.


--- The testament of Alexander Fletcher_1 [Оригинал [Оригинал.txt].txt].txt ---

[4] The Key L107
My lot was made bearable only by the goal to which my work would lead, and surely a lifelong dedication to scholastic discipline did much to mitigate the spiritual degradation inescapably concomitant with the magical practices I undertook after a lengthy study of the manuscript I had borne away from that isolated manor house. That my praxis resulted in real, perceptible, and physical effects I could not deny, and it was with a mixture of elation and disgust that I regarded the results of my first operations: elation because I knew that I had now come into possession of the key that would unlock the means to my revenge, disgust because I had now become a member of a corrupt brotherhood of cultic ignorance, one that linked with repugnant intimacy the jungle savage and the educated practitioner, and united the degenerate slum dweller with the elegant sophisticate in an incestuous amalgam of deviant methodology. Nor did I refrain from seizing every available opportunity to add to my knowledge and my practice, for the manuscript, while quite usable in its own fashion, contained only the most basic of the skills I would eventually require.

--- The_Case_of_Charles_Dexter_Ward_The_H.P._Lovecraft_Wiki_Fandom_abd28ac330.txt ---

[1] Yog-Sothoth L339
Horror historian Les Daniels called The Case of Charles Dexter Ward Lovecraft's "finest novel". E. F. Bleiler noted that the short novel, "despite its being strangely tired and routine, has interesting concepts and good moments". Baird Searles found that "HPL's great knowledge of New England history provides a convincing background" for the story. Douglas Robillard stated Lovecraft's negative assessment of The Case of Charles Dexter Ward was "too harsh; this is one of his finest works". Cthulhu Mythos[] Charles Dexter Ward contains the first mention of the Cthulhu Mythos entity Yog-Sothoth, who appears repeatedly as an element in an incantation. Joseph Curwen is the owner of a copy of the Necronomicon (disguised as a book labelled Qanoon-e-Islam) and there are hints of cult activities in a fishing village that refer obliquely to the events narrated in "The Festival". The story also contains references to the Dream Cycle: Dr. Willett notices the "Sign of Koth" chiselled above a doorway, and remembers his friend Randolph Carter drawing the sign and explaining its powers and meaning. First appearance of the Dragon's Head and Dragon's Tail signs.

[2] Yog-Sothoth L343
Joseph Curwen is the owner of a copy of the Necronomicon (disguised as a book labelled Qanoon-e-Islam) and there are hints of cult activities in a fishing village that refer obliquely to the events narrated in "The Festival".
